title: Best Fake Security Cameras That Actually Deter Crime
excerpt: When dummy cameras deter thieves and when they fail: placement rules, realism details, warning signs, and pairing decoys with one real camera.
body:
Here is the honest answer up front: a fake camera can discourage a casual opportunist, and it does nothing against anyone who tests it. Whether a dummy earns its place depends on where you put it, how convincing it looks at a glance, and — most importantly — whether at least one real camera backs it up. This guide shows how to get genuine deterrent value out of decoys without fooling yourself about what they are.

A dummy camera is theatre. Theatre works on passers-by scanning for easy targets, and it fails the moment someone needs evidence. Keep both truths in mind and every decision below follows naturally.

What a dummy camera can and cannot do

A convincing dummy changes the calculation of the casual thief — the opportunist checking for unlocked sheds or lifting parcels chooses quickly and moves on from houses that look watched. Against that audience, a well-placed decoy with a warning sign genuinely helps. What it cannot do is record. After a break-in, a dummy contributes no faces, no times, no number plates — and it may have displaced a real camera in the budget that would have. Buy dummies as a supplement to real coverage, never as the coverage itself.

Where decoys fool people — and where they get spotted

Decoys work at distance and fail up close. A dummy mounted high above a driveway reads as real to anyone scanning from the street, because nobody studies a camera from twenty metres. The same dummy at head height beside a front door invites inspection — and inspection kills it, since plastic, a painted lens, and a wobbling bracket betray themselves up close. So place decoys high, overlooking approaches and parking spots where their audience stays far away. Never place one where it must survive close scrutiny: beside entry keypads or at eye level where a visitor waits with nothing to do but look at it. Positions that need evidence — above the till, facing the car, covering the gate people use — belong to real cameras. For those spots, see our outdoor camera guide.

The details that separate a convincing dummy from a toy

Real cameras share a visual language, and a decoy must speak it fluently. Work through this list before mounting anything:

  • Lens realism: a recessed dark glass circle with visible depth, not a flat printed dot. Depth is the hardest detail to fake and the first thing eyes check.
  • Cabling: run a short length of cable or conduit from the dummy into the wall or eaves. A camera floating with no wire trail is a giveaway.
  • Mounting hardware: proper screws, a level bracket, a position a real installer would choose — under eaves, at a corner covering two approaches.
  • Status light behaviour: a slow, irregular blink reads as a recording indicator; a frantic strobe reads as a toy. Better still, switch it off — many real cameras show no light at all.
  • Weathering: a gleaming new unit among year-old gutters draws the eye for the wrong reason. Dull the shine so it matches its surroundings.

Pairing one real camera with visible decoys

The classic arrangement is one real camera doing the quiet work while dummies do the advertising. Mount the real camera discreetly — tucked under eaves with a clean view of faces or plates — and place dummies where they are seen first: the street-facing corner, above the garage. An intruder who spots the dummies and keeps their head down still walks through the real camera's frame. This is also the economical answer for larger properties: real coverage where evidence matters, theatre everywhere else. Our no-subscription guide keeps the real camera's running costs down.

Keep the secret narrow

The arrangement works only while observers assume every camera is real. Limit that knowledge to the household — and know exactly which unit is real and how to pull its clips under pressure.

Signs, lights, and cable stubs: cheap realism that works

A weatherproof warning sign at the gate does more deterrent work than upgrading the dummy itself, because most decisions to move on happen at the boundary. A motion-triggered floodlight above the decoy sells the illusion brilliantly: visitors link light and camera in their minds, and the light itself is a genuine deterrent. Small touches compound it — a cable stub in the masonry, a second dummy covering the first one's blind side.

The maintenance the theatre needs

A dead blinking light, a dummy hanging crooked after a storm, a sign faded to blank plastic — neglected theatre advertises absence, not vigilance. Twice a year, straighten mounts, replace LED batteries, and renew signage. Ten minutes keeps the story believable.

When to skip fakes and buy the real thing

Skip the dummy when any of these apply: you have already been targeted and need evidence next time; the position covers vehicle access where plates matter; an insurer or police report will ask for footage; or the camera must watch a vulnerable person or a cash-handling spot. In those cases a decoy is worse than nothing, spending budget and effort while delivering zero proof. One real camera with local recording over the door beats three dummies on every wall — deterrence you can also rewind.

The rule of thumb: decoys may stop the opportunist, only recordings settle the argument afterwards. Let dummies advertise, let one real camera remember, and never confuse the two jobs.
